lead: A traverse is a chain of straight lines measured between stations. Each line is fixed by its length and its bearing. Latitude and departure split that line into a north-south part and an east-west part. The split turns slanted lines into signed numbers that add like vectors. Surveyors use it to carry coordinates along roads, canals, boundaries and control networks, and to check that a closed traverse returns to its starting point.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.1 for whole circle bearings and Unit 1 for trigonometric ratios and coordinate axes.

blocks.text: A traverse is a survey made of connected straight lines. The ends of the lines are traverse stations. For every line the surveyor records the length and the bearing. The chain of lines is the traverse.

A closed traverse starts and ends at the same station. It encloses an area, so it suits a plot boundary or a lake. An open traverse starts at a known station and ends at an unknown point. Roads, canals and pipelines use it because the route does not return. A link traverse starts at one known station and ends at a different known station. It joins two control points.

In all three types, the field record is a traverse table. Each row is one line: from station, to station, length and bearing. Two computed columns are added next: latitude and departure. These columns turn each slanted line into a north-south step and an east-west step, so the steps can be added and checked.

sections.h3: Latitude and departure from a bearing

blocks.text: Take a line of length l metres. Its whole circle bearing is θ, measured clockwise from north. Latitude is the north-south component. Departure is the east-west component.
Latitude = l cos θ    Departure = l sin θ
blocks.where: l is the line length in metres; θ is the whole circle bearing in degrees, clockwise from north; latitude is positive north and negative south; departure is positive east and negative west.

blocks.text: The sign follows the quadrant. In the north-east quadrant both are positive. In the south-east, latitude is negative and departure positive. In the south-west, both are negative. In the north-west, latitude is positive and departure negative.

A reduced bearing α is the acute angle from the nearer north or south end of the meridian, measured towards east or west. Reduced bearings give the same numbers if you keep the signs separate. For α (0° to 90°), latitude is ± l cos α and departure is ± l sin α. Choose + or − from the north/south and east/west words. Do not put a reduced bearing into l cos θ and l sin θ: θ must be the whole circle bearing, otherwise the signs come out wrong. A line at 135° has latitude 180 cos 135° = −127.28 m and departure 180 sin 135° = +127.28 m.

sections.h3: Traverse table, coordinates and the closure checks

blocks.text: A traverse table has one row per line. The columns are line, length l, whole circle bearing θ, latitude l cos θ and departure l sin θ. Add the signed latitudes and the signed departures in separate columns.
Coordinates come from those sums. Start at a station with known coordinates (E₀, N₀). For each line, add its departure to easting and its latitude to northing:
These are consecutive coordinates. They depend on the starting station. Independent coordinates are tied to a survey grid, so every station has one fixed pair.
For a closed traverse, the return to the first station gives two checks:

blocks.where: Σ latitude is the algebraic sum of all signed latitudes in metres; Σ departure is the algebraic sum of all signed departures in metres.

blocks.text: If either sum is not zero, the traverse has a misclosure: the amount by which the sums fail to be zero. Adjusting it is the job of Chapter 2.5. An open traverse has no such check because it does not return to the start. Area from the coordinates is in Chapter 2.6.

figure.caption: Each line is split into a north-south latitude and an east-west departure; the last row gives the signed sums, which are not zero, so the closed traverse has a misclosure. Individual entries are rounded to whole metres (the DA bearing is 303°20′ in the worked example), while the worked example uses unrounded values.

spec.title: Traverse ABCD: length (m), bearing, latitude (m), departure (m)

examples.question: A closed traverse ABCD has AB = 200 m at 45°, BC = 180 m at 135°, CD = 160 m at 210° and DA = 226 m at 303°20′. Compute the latitude and departure of every line and the two sums. Does the traverse close exactly?
steps: Use θ as the whole circle bearing. For each line: latitude = l cos θ and departure = l sin θ.
AB: latitude = 200 cos 45° = +141.42 m; departure = 200 sin 45° = +141.42 m.
BC: latitude = 180 cos 135° = −127.28 m; departure = 180 sin 135° = +127.28 m.
CD: latitude = 160 cos 210° = −138.56 m; departure = 160 sin 210° = −80.00 m.
examples.answer: Σ latitude = −0.23 m and Σ departure = −0.12 m; neither is zero, so the traverse does not close exactly.
examples.check:
import math
lines = [(200, 45), (180, 135), (160, 210), (226, 303 + 20/60)]
sum_lat = 0.0
sum_dep = 0.0
for l, b in lines:
    r = math.radians(b)
    lat = l * math.cos(r)
    dep = l * math.sin(r)
    print(f"{lat:.2f}")
    print(f"{dep:.2f}")
    sum_lat += lat
    sum_dep += dep
print(f"{sum_lat:.2f}")
print(f"{sum_dep:.2f}")

traps: Using a reduced bearing in l cos θ and l sin θ. The formula needs the whole circle bearing θ; a reduced bearing gives the wrong sign in the south or west half.
Forgetting that latitude is north-south and departure is east-west. Swapping them turns every coordinate step by 90°.
Dropping the sign when adding. Latitudes and departures are signed vector components, not plain lengths, so −127.28 m must stay negative in the sum.
Applying the zero-sum check to an open traverse. Only a closed traverse must return to the start; an open traverse has no such condition.
Treating a nonzero sum as proof that the fieldwork is wrong. It is a misclosure, and it is adjusted in Chapter 2.5; the sum itself must still be computed and reported.

quiz.q: Define latitude and departure of a traverse line.
quiz.a: For length l and whole circle bearing θ, latitude = l cos θ (north-south component) and departure = l sin θ (east-west component). Both carry signs.

quiz.q: Why must a closed traverse have Σ latitude = 0 and Σ departure = 0?
quiz.a: Returning to the start means the total north-south change and total east-west change are both zero. The signed components cancel.

quiz.q: A line is 150 m long at a whole circle bearing of 120°. Compute its latitude and departure.
quiz.a: Latitude = 150 cos 120° = −75.00 m; departure = 150 sin 120° = +129.90 m.

quiz.q: A line is 80 m long at 240°. Compute its latitude and departure.
quiz.a: Latitude = 80 cos 240° = −40.00 m; departure = 80 sin 240° = −69.28 m.

quiz.q: A student has a line of 100 m at 150°. The reduced bearing is 30°. The student writes latitude = +86.60 m and departure = +50.00 m. Explain the error and give the correct values.
quiz.a: The student used the reduced bearing in l cos θ and l sin θ. For 150° the line is south-east: latitude = 100 cos 150° = −86.60 m, departure = 100 sin 150° = +50.00 m. The departure is right; the latitude sign is wrong.

quiz.q: What are the signs of latitude and departure for a line in the north-west quadrant?
A closed traverse has Σ latitude = +0.24 m and Σ departure = −0.18 m. What do these two numbers tell you? Do not adjust.
quiz.a: The traverse does not close exactly. The total north-south change is 0.24 m and total east-west change is −0.18 m. Both should be zero for exact closure; the nonzero values are the misclosure components.

quiz.q: Station P has coordinates E = 1000.00 m, N = 2000.00 m. A line from P has latitude +60.00 m and departure −25.00 m. Find the coordinates of the next station.

beyond: Not for the exam. Total stations and GNSS receivers compute latitudes, departures and coordinates inside the instrument. Field software then adjusts the traverse by least squares rather than by a simple rule. GIS and cadastral systems store the resulting coordinates as the parcel boundary. Search for traverse computation, coordinate geometry in surveying, and least-squares traverse adjustment.
